faqs.question: Which Purana tells the Ganesh Chaturthi story?
faqs.answer: Several do, and they disagree. The Shiva Purana's Kumara Khanda chapter 13 is the best known, but the Skanda, Linga, Matsya and Brahmavaivarta Puranas each give a different birth, and the moon curse sits in the Ganesha Purana instead.

faqs.question: Did Parvati create Ganesha on her own?
faqs.answer: In the Shiva Purana and the Skanda Purana, yes: she makes him from the dirt of her own body with no help from Shiva. The Linga Purana disagrees and has him born from Parvati's womb as a portion of Shiva's own power.

faqs.question: Who actually cut off Ganesha's head?
faqs.answer: Shiva, in the version the Shiva Purana chooses to narrate. Verse 5 of that same chapter names another aeon in which Shani's glance does it, and the Brahmavaivarta Purana's Ganesha Khanda places a discourse between Parvati and Shani before the head is lost.

faqs.question: Is the Vinayaka Vratha Katha the same as the Ganesh Chaturthi katha?
faqs.answer: It is the South Indian form of it, and it is longer. The Telugu, Kannada and Tamil reading adds the moon curse and Krishna's false accusation to the birth story, and it is treated as part of the vratam rather than as background to it.

faqs.question: What should I do if I have already seen the moon on Ganesh Chaturthi?
faqs.answer: The customary remedy is to hear or recite the Syamantaka story, which is why it got bundled into the vratha katha in the first place. The Ganesha Purana does not prescribe that: its chapter 61 ends with the moon propitiating Ganesha and the curse being limited rather than removed.

faqs.question: Why is the moon allowed on Sankashti Chaturthi but not on Ganesh Chaturthi?
faqs.answer: Because the same chapter says so. Ganesha Purana, Upasana Khanda 61, verses 48 and 49, tell the moon that on the krishna-paksha chaturthi he must be looked at with effort, and that reversing the two makes the vrata worthless.

faqs.question: Is the story of Krishna and the Syamantaka jewel part of the Ganesh Chaturthi katha?
faqs.answer: In the vernacular vratha katha, yes. In the source texts, no: the Bhagavata Purana's Syamantaka chapters 10.56 and 10.57 contain no moon, no chaturthi and no Ganesha, and the word syamantaka never appears in the Ganesha Purana.

faqs.question: Is the Ganesha Purana one of the eighteen Mahapuranas?
faqs.answer: No. Michael's 1983 survey classes it as an Upa-Purana, composed along with the Ganapati Upanishad specifically to praise Ganapati. It is still a large text, with 92 chapters in the Upasana Khanda and 155 in the Krida Khanda.

faqs.question: Why does Ganesha have only one tusk?
faqs.answer: That has competing answers too. The Brahmavaivarta Purana's Ganesha Khanda takes it up in chapter XXIV alongside a discourse between Jamadagni and Kartavirya, rather than through the familiar story about writing down the Mahabharata.

faqs.question: Can I read the katha in English instead of Sanskrit?
faqs.answer: Yes. The vrat-katha genre has always travelled in whatever language the household speaks, which is why Telugu, Marathi, Kannada and Hindi versions exist at all. Reading it aloud in English keeps the part that matters, which is that it is read.

faqs.question: Is there a Ganesh Chaturthi story in Hindi I can read to children?
faqs.answer: The usual Hindi katha runs to three or four short paragraphs: the birth, the beheading, the elephant head and the moon, read before the aarti. It is the same material as the longer southern version, cut to a length a child will sit through.

faqs.question: Does the katha have to be read at a particular time?
faqs.answer: It is read with the puja, which is timed to Madhyahna because Ganesha is held to have been born at midday. For Pune in 2026 that window is 11:16 AM to 1:44 PM on Monday 14 September.

# The Ganesh Chaturthi Story, and Why the Puranas Disagree

There is no single Ganesh Chaturthi story. The Shiva, Skanda, Linga, Matsya and Brahmavaivarta Puranas each give a different account of how Ganesha was born and how he lost his head, and the Shiva Purana openly concedes that it is telling only one of several. Ganesh Chaturthi 2026 falls on Monday 14 September, with visarjan on Friday 25 September.

We build shareable celebration pages, so the katha reaches us as something people retell rather than something they read: across all 3,860 pages SubhSandesh has created since March 2026, spanning 15 page types, 49.6% are opened on a phone (22,667 of 45,656 views) and 96.1% of started pages are actually published and shared (3,708 of 3,860). Both are platform-wide figures across those 15 page types, not Ganesh-specific ones. Below: each version with its source text, the chapter behind the moon prohibition, and what the Vinayaka Vratha Katha is for. 

## What the Ganesh Chaturthi katha is

The Ganesh Chaturthi katha is the narrative recited as part of the festival's vrata: the birth of Ganesha, the loss of his head, the elephant head that replaces it, and in the south the moon's curse. It is a ritual text, not a bedtime story, and in this genre the reading is itself the act.

Different regions read different kathas under the same name. A Marathi household on 14 September 2026 usually hears the birth narrative alone; a Telugu or Kannada household reading the Vinayaka Vratha Katha hears the moon curse and Krishna's false accusation too, closing with akshata placed on the head.

## Six tellings of how Ganesha got his head

Each account states who makes the child, what he is made from, and how the head is lost. S. M. Michael's survey in [Asian Folklore Studies 42, 1983](https://asianethnology.org/article/148337-the-origin-of-the-ganapati-cult) puts it bluntly: the Puranic explanation of Ganapati's origin is confusing and contradictory.

### 1. Shiva Purana: Parvati's own body, and Shiva's blade

In the [Shiva Purana's Kumara Khanda, chapter 13](https://www.wisdomlib.org/hinduism/book/shiva-purana-english/d/doc226133.html), Parvati's companions Jaya and Vijaya point out that every gana in the house answers to Shiva and she has no attendant of her own. She makes a boy from the dirt of her own body and posts him at the door while she bathes. Shiva arrives, is refused entry, and beheads him; an elephant's head replaces the lost one.

### 2. Shiva Purana again: Shani's glance, in another aeon

Verse 5 of that same chapter says the birth is told differently in different kalpas, and names a version in which the child is born of the great lord and it is **Shani's** look that severs the head. The text then narrates the Shvetakalpa account instead. A Purana conceding in its fifth verse that its own version is one of several is not a detail the festival listicles carry.

### 3. Skanda Purana: Parvati alone

Michael records that the Skanda Purana ascribes the birth to Parvati alone, with no part played by Shiva. The same text promotes Ganapati to an avatara rather than a household guardian, which is a different theological job from the one the Shiva Purana gives him.

### 4. Linga Purana: a portion of Shiva, born from Parvati

Here the direction reverses. An amsha, a portion of Shiva's own power, takes handsome form and is delivered from Parvati's womb. No clay, no dirt from the bath, no doorway confrontation.

### 5. Matsya Purana: bath oils and Ganges water

Parvati, bathing, gathers the oil, ointments and impurity coming off her body into the figure of a man, then animates it with Ganges water. A neighbouring version has her make the elephant-headed rakshasi Malini drink that mixture; Malini conceives, and Parvati takes the child.

### 6. Brahmavaivarta Purana: a vow, a boon from Krishna, and Shani

The Ganesha Khanda of the Brahmavaivarta Purana, in Rajendra Nath Sen's 1922 translation for the Sacred Books of the Hindus, does not begin with clay. Chapters III to VII have Parvati perform the Punyaka vrata to propitiate Krishna, chapter VIII is the birth of Ganesha, chapter XI a discourse between Parvati and Shani, chapter XX the reason he was given an elephant's face. Shiva is not the one who takes the head.

## The five Puranas side by side

The five Puranic accounts, reduced to the three things they actually disagree about.

| Text | Who makes the child | Made from | How the head is lost |
|---|---|---|---|
| Shiva Purana, Kumara Khanda 13 | Parvati, alone | The dirt of her own body | Shiva beheads him at the door |
| Shiva Purana, variant named at 13.5 | The great lord | Not stated | Shani's glance severs it |
| Skanda Purana | Parvati, alone | Not stated | Not part of this account |
| Linga Purana | An amsha of Shiva | Shiva's own power | Not part of this account |
| Matsya Purana | Parvati, while bathing | Bath oils, ointments, body impurity, Ganges water | Not part of this account |

The beheading is not a fixed part of the story. Three of these five accounts omit it, and the one text that tells it twice names two different culprits.

## When these texts were written

Ganesha is late. Michael quotes Coomaraswamy that Ganesha does not appear in iconography before the Gupta period, R. G. Bhandarkar that the cult must have come into practice between the end of the fifth century and the end of the eighth, and P. V. Kane that his characteristics were fixed before the fifth or sixth century.

The Ganesha Purana is later still, and enormous. Counting chapter colophons in the [Sanskrit text of its Upasana Khanda](https://sanskritdocuments.org/doc_purana/gaNeshapurANam1.html) gives 92 chapters, and the Krida Khanda 155: 247 chapters for a text devoted to one deity.

## Why you should not look at the moon on Ganesh Chaturthi

Chapter 61 of the Ganesha Purana's Upasana Khanda is titled chandra-shapa-anugraha-varnanam, the description of the moon's curse and its lifting. Ganapati loses a disputed fruit to Kumara, takes a terrifying form and obstructs Brahma's work; the moon laughs; Ganesha curses him to be unfit to look upon, and whoever sees him a great sinner.

Verse 25 is the operative one: on Bhadrapada shukla chaturthi, knowingly or unknowingly, seeing the moon brings the curse and heavy suffering. Verses 46 and 47 name the penalties as abhishapa, papa, hani and murkhata — false accusation, sin, loss, foolishness. For Pune in 2026, Drik Panchang gives the window to avoid as [9:06 AM to 8:34 PM on 14 September](https://www.drikpanchang.com/festivals/ganesh-chaturthi/ganesh-chaturthi-date-time.html?geoname-id=1259229&year=2026), 11 hours 28 minutes, with the Madhyahna puja muhurat at 11:16 AM to 1:44 PM.

Two things the popular telling gets wrong. The quarrel here is over a fruit, not a tumble off the mouse after too many modaks, and no tusk is thrown. The Syamantaka jewel is absent too: syamantaka occurs zero times in either khanda.

The reverse also holds. The Syamantaka episode sits in the Bhagavata Purana at 10.56 and 10.57, and a search of the [Sanskrit text of those chapters](https://gretil.sub.uni-goettingen.de/gretil/corpustei/transformations/plaintext/sa_bhAgavatapurANa.txt) finds no candra, no caturthi and no Ganesha. Krishna being accused because he saw the moon on Ganesh Chaturthi is a join made later, in the vrata-katha tradition, not by either Purana.

The same chapter explains Sankashti. Verses 48 and 49 say the krishna-paksha chaturthi moon must instead be looked at with effort, and that reversing the two makes the vrata worthless. That is why a Sankashti fast breaks at moonrise while Ganesh Chaturthi hides from it.

## The Vinayaka Vratha Katha, and why it is read out loud

In Telugu, Kannada and Tamil households the Vinayaka Vratha Katha is not colour around the puja. The reading is a component of the vratam, it closes with akshata placed on the head, and an observance without it is treated as unfinished.

That is a property of the genre. In a study of the Swasthani Vrat Katha in the [Journal of the University of Ruhuna, December 2024](https://jur.sljol.info/articles/10.4038/jur.v12i2.8054), R. P. Adhikary describes a month-long Magh observance in which fasting, prayer and recitation are one practice, and argues the recitation is what carries the tradition between generations.

A Hindi reader usually gets a shorter katha: birth, beheading and moon in three or four paragraphs, read before the aarti. Same material at a different length.

If you are sending the katha rather than reading it in the same room, format matters more than wording. A [Ganesh Chaturthi page the recipient performs themselves](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-ganesh-chaturthi) — offering the durva, kumkum, flowers and modak, circling the aarti thali, writing their own prarthana back — gives them something to do with the story instead of text to scroll past. Across SubhSandesh's 15 page types, 42.1% of creators password-protect a page before sharing it, 1,625 of 3,860, again a platform-wide figure.

| Way to send it | What it costs | What the reader needs | Platform-wide SubhSandesh data |
|---|---|---|---|
| Read aloud at the mandap | Nothing | To be in the room | Not applicable |
| Forward a vratha kalpam PDF | Nothing | 15-plus pages of patience | Not applicable |
| Paste the katha into WhatsApp | Nothing | Tolerance for a text wall | Not applicable |
| Send a page they perform | Free | A phone and a link | 49.6% of shared pages open on a phone; 96.1% get published |

Only the last row carries numbers, and they are platform-wide across all 15 page types: the Ganesh template shipped days ago and has created no pages yet.

## Where a shared page cannot carry the katha

A page cannot perform the vratam. It cannot put akshata on anyone's head, hand anyone a modak, or stand in for the mandap when the aarti starts on 14 September. If the person you have in mind is in the next room, close the laptop.

It is also the wrong container for a full text: a Vinayaka Vratha Kalpam runs to fifteen pages or more with the puja vidhanam, the 21 patri and the katha, and that belongs in a booklet. A page does the short version well, and for occasions this template does not fit, the [full SubhSandesh template library](https://subhsandesh.in/templates) is the better starting point.

## Watch the page get built

Ninety seconds, start to finish — the aarti going round, the five offerings, and the box at the end where they write a line back to you: [Ganesh Chaturthi Wishes Online — Full Walkthrough](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mpWiv5T59QY). More page walkthroughs on Instagram: [@subhsandesh_official](https://www.instagram.com/subhsandesh_official).

auditReport.honestAssessment: It is the only page in these SERPs that names the source text behind each version of the Ganesha birth story and says where they contradict: the Shiva Purana conceding at 13.5 that its own account is one of several, three of five Puranic accounts containing no beheading at all, and the moon prohibition traced to Ganesha Purana, Upasana Khanda 61 with the Sanskrit verses cited. Two textual checks in it appear nowhere else on the web that I could find: the word syamantaka occurs zero times in either khanda of the Ganesha Purana, and the Bhagavata Purana's Syamantaka chapters 10.56-57 contain no moon, no chaturthi and no Ganesha, which means the familiar combined katha is a later join. Against that: the domain has no Ganesha authority at all, this is a mythology query where Britannica, museum sites and Isha rank on brand rather than accuracy, and the first-party data is platform-wide across 15 page types because the Ganesh template has created zero pages, so it supports the sharing section and nothing about the myth. The primary internal link is also 404 as of 2026-09-09. Expect months, and expect the citation value here to come from answer engines quoting the chapter references rather than from ranking.
